name: Quill
workload: Frontend call latency of LOG_INFO with two ints and a double, 1 thread and 4 threads, async logging
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: 6 ns median / 6 ns p90 / 9 ns p99.9 vs spdlog 271 / 296 / 360 ns; 4 threads: 8 ns median vs spdlog 557 ns (about 45x lower median latency, derived from page data)
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, tuned (isolcpus, nohz_full)
tradeoffs: Formatting deferred to a backend thread; log arguments copied to a per-thread queue; extra backend thread; arguments must be copyable or have codec; ordering/crash-loss caveats of async logging.
caveats: Benchmark table written by the Quill author (also the harness author); measures frontend latency only, not end-to-end throughput; tuned system with isolated cores and mitigations off; README states 6.44M msg/s throughput to file (not compared to spdlog in snippet read). Last commit date not seen.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Show HN faster logging library than spdlog' (thread 'Nanolog supports logging with 7 ns median latency' discussion mentions Quill); README opened on github.com

name: fmtlog
workload: Frontend latency and throughput logging NanoLog message set with spdlog default header pattern (spdlog basic_logger_st baseline)
claimed_speedup: 6.2-6.4 ns per call vs spdlog 156-391 ns (README bench table); Quill table 1 thread: 6 ns vs spdlog 271 ns
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, tuned (isolcpus, nohz_full) (README bench: Xeon Gold 6144 3.5 GHz)
tradeoffs: Needs fmt; per-thread SPSC queue 1 MB; drops messages when queue is full unless FMTLOG_BLOCK; background thread must poll; static info table adds code size per log site.
caveats: Own README bench vs synchronous spdlog single-threaded logger; compiler flags not stated in README; the A tier rests on the Quill author's public benchmark (odygrd/logger_benchmarks, GCC 14.2, i5-12600). Throughput is only 2.6-7 M/s, comparable to spdlog's 2.6-6.4 M/s, so the win is latency not throughput.
found_via: Hacker News: NanoLog and spdlog threads pointed to low-latency loggers; repo README opened on github.com

name: XTR
workload: Frontend latency of logging two ints and a double, 1 and 4 threads
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: 6 ns median vs spdlog 271 ns; 4 threads: 8 ns median vs spdlog 557 ns (Quill README table)
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, tuned (isolcpus, nohz_full)
tradeoffs: Low-latency/real-time design, no allocation or syscalls in the log call; asynchronous; Linux/FreeBSD focus; strings copied to queue.
caveats: Number is from the Quill author's benchmark, not XTR's own README (README shows its own ns-level google-benchmark numbers without spdlog comparison). Frontend latency only.
found_via: Hacker News: low-latency C++ logger threads; XTR row found in Quill README table

name: NanoLog (PlatformLab)
workload: Median/p99.9 invocation latency for six log messages, plus throughput 1-16 threads, vs spdlog 1.1.0, glog 0.3.5, Log4j2, Boost, ETW
claimed_speedup: 7 ns median vs spdlog 214 ns and glog 1198 ns (staticString); README claims over 80 million logs/s; Quill table 1 thread: 8 ns vs spdlog 271 ns
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, tuned (isolcpus, nohz_full)
license: BSD-3-Clause (unconfirmed from page, LICENSE file present)
tradeoffs: Binary log output needs a separate decompressor to read logs; Linux only; preprocessor version needs Python script in build; C++17 version is a library; POSIX AIO.
caveats: Own README table uses old spdlog v1.1.0 and glog 0.3.5; hardware not read; A tier rests on the Quill README table (public code, GCC 14.2, i5-12600) which has NanoLog at 8 ns vs spdlog 271 ns. Throughput not comparable to text loggers because output is binary. License identifier and last commit date not confirmed.
found_via: Hacker News: 'Nanolog supports logging with 7 ns median latency' and 'NanoLog' (item 20853586)

name: binlog (Morgan Stanley)
workload: Frontend latency of two ints and a double, 1 and 4 threads
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: 18 ns median vs spdlog 271 ns; 4 threads: 29 ns vs spdlog 557 ns (Quill README table)
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, tuned (isolcpus, nohz_full)
tradeoffs: Binary log format, needs bread/binlog tools to read; async via lock-free queue; C++14.
caveats: Own README gives only own ns numbers ('not for direct comparison', Xeon E5-2698, RHEL 2.6.32) with no spdlog comparison; win comes from the Quill author's benchmark. Repo page not opened with WebFetch, only README via raw.githubusercontent.com; license, stars and date unverified.
found_via: Hacker News: low-latency C++ logger discussions; row found in Quill README table

name: BqLog
workload: 10 threads, 2M entries each, compressed log format vs spdlog async, glog, Log4j2, fmtlog, quill
claimed_speedup: README: 6-65x faster than spdlog (async); 47-252x faster than glog; 7-18x faster than quill; but Quill README table has BqLog at 125 ns vs Quill 6 ns frontend latency
tradeoffs: Compressed binary format, multi-language wrappers (Java, C#, Python, Go, TS), encryption option; heavier library.
caveats: Numbers seen only via repo page summary; docs/BENCHMARK.md not opened. Measures throughput with its own harness; independent Quill table shows BqLog slower than Quill, fmtlog and XTR on frontend latency, so the claim is workload-specific. Last commit not seen.
found_via: Hacker News: low-latency logging threads; repo page opened on github.com

name: NanoLog (Iyengar111)
workload: Latency percentiles for 1 and 4 threads vs spdlog and g3log
claimed_speedup: 1 thread median 0 us vs spdlog 3 us; 4 threads about 0.6 us average vs spdlog 1.8 us (README)
tradeoffs: Guaranteed or non-guaranteed (ring buffer, may drop) modes; C++11 header and source; no binary format.
caveats: First-party microsecond-resolution table; old spdlog version; Quill table gives this logger 106 ns vs spdlog 271 ns, only 2.5x. License and last commit not confirmed; likely stale.
found_via: Hacker News: 'NanoLog' discussions; repo page opened on github.com
